name: Name
body:
Malekus chose a seat in one of the temple’s back pews. He didn’t wear the mask or armor of his station, wanting to be as one of the congregation. He was conscious of his bulk and attempted to make himself appear smaller as he settled into his seat.
The temple was a vast structure of sandstone arches. Like the ribs of a leviathan, the central chamber of the temple loomed high overhead, buttressed by pillars of yellowish stone. Between each rib, there were colorful windows of pewter and stained glass. These depicted pivotal moments of the faith: the Molgur barbarians’ blood spilt by the blade of Geth. Fields of wheat growing in ordered rows. The fire of the priest-kings leaving barbarian mobs as scorched corpses, wrought in glass stained purple and black. Before, these would have been polished each morning by throngs of widows and fatherless children, but now they were allowed to gather dust. Panels depicting divine scenes hung cracked or empty, allowing windborne sand to infiltrate the holy space.

name: Name
body: The man known as the Burning Truth sighed and eased back into his pew. He let his eyes fall shut and listened to the wind's rise and fall as it played through the gaps in the glass, the patter of grains of sand hitting them and slithering in, forming pillowy dunes in the abandoned hall. The susurrus reminded him of the sound of a congregation, the soft hush of robes shuffling, the faint sounds of breaths taken in awe. "This is where I heard my first true sermon," he said, opening his eyes and addressing the space behind the altar. "Back when I escaped Caspia, I sat right here and listened to you speak passages of the True Law. Your words ignited the fire within me that my previous life had so smothered. "You spoke about the nobility of suffering in the Lawgiver’s Name," Malekus continued, rising from the pew. "How every pain we endured for him brought joy to Menoth’s heart and fueled the fire that cleansed the impurities of our souls. I had suffered so much pain, so much misery, so much loss. Learning that it had a purpose uplifted me. Having people just like me— each imperfect and hurting individual who made up the masses—having a family uplifted me."

name: Name
body: Malekus walked down the center aisle, trailing the thick, slack fingers of his hand across the backs of the empty pews. He did this without thinking. It was as if the altar had a magnetic pull on him. The closer he got, the stronger it became. He was drawn along until he stood before the altar, where he was compelled to his knees, his head bowed in reverence. He knelt there for a time. His breath began to quicken and shudder. Before long, he was holding back searing tears, trying to suppress his sobs. "Why?" he whispered. Then, looking up past the altar to the Menofix mounted on the wall behind it, he repeated, "Why?" He waited, chest heaving in the hush of the temple. His question, first spoken to a memory of the priest who had once stood behind that altar, then transformed into a plea to the god to whom he had dedicated his life. The echo of his voice faded into the high arches, mingling with the hiss of wind through the broken panes of glass. Swirling sand danced in thin beams of sunlight. There was no answer—only the sigh of wind and the faint rasp of sand against stone.

name: Name
body:
He whispered again, "Why have you let us come to this?"
He knelt there, his hands clenched into fists. The hush of the temple enveloped him, a sickening reminder of how it once thrummed with fervent voices reciting liturgy, the chorus of hymns rising to the heavens, and the clang of censer chains. He remembered the scents of incense carried in thick curls of smoke; now, the only scent was that of the dust of neglect.
When Malekus was a boy, everything he knew was filtered through the cruel lens of the orphanage in Caspia. There, attended by Morrow’s devout believers, he and the other children were treated with suspicion and fear, subjected to cruelties for the slightest misstep. But he found escape from that dark, oppressive place through the purity of fire, learning from a traveling priest who spoke of a stern but just god. One who demanded sacrifice yet gave meaning to suffering. That seed of devotion had quietly sprouted in Malekus’s heart, unwatered as he fled the streets of Caspia and came upon this very temple.

name: Name
body: And that was where his life changed forever. Here, in the hush of these sandstone arches, he listened to a sermon that made him weep with relief. You suffer, child, but that suffering has purpose. The priest’s words had been like hot oil poured over a raw wound— searing yet somehow healing as well. Malekus’s spirit had blazed with conviction, a living fire igniting inside him. This temple had once been filled with pilgrims like him: the maimed, the outcast, the grieving—all who needed the Lawbringer’s guiding flame. The young Malekus had felt united with them, shoulder to shoulder in adoration of the Creator who shaped humanity from rough sand and demanded only their loyalty in return. It was a faith steeped in discipline, duty, and the acceptance of the righteous burdens which all living people were sworn to bear. In the years since, that bright flame of unity had flickered. The priests—some hungry for power, others so rigid in their dogma that they refused to see the world changing around them—had unknowingly sown seeds of discord. Trust had crumbled, and the faithful turned against one another. Malekus had done his duty. He had followed the words of the True Law as recited by the priests and all those who demonstrated the authority to speak with the Creator’s voice. He had strapped on his armor, taken up blade and fire, and set out to purge anyone who threatened the faith. And he had watched as, with a heartbreaking inevitability, the faithful turned against the faithful until the entire realm fell into chaos.

name: Name
body: Now Malekus sat alone in the ravaged temple. The multicolored glass was half-shattered, and the intricate pewter leading was blackened by neglect. The Menofix behind the altar—once a beloved piece of flawless bronze craftsmanship—had tarnished to a patchy, dull gray. Whether due to the desert air or the lack of upkeep, it appeared as though the holy symbol itself had withered in sorrow. Malekus clenched his jaw, tears wet on his cheeks. "All that we endured… all those battles. Were they fought in your name, or the name of those with a lust for power?" He bowed his head and squeezed his eyes shut, allowing himself to remember. There were always more battles swirling in his mind than he had the strength to face: the storms of war and interrogation, the screams of heretics. Or those labeled heretics by the scrutators—he had never questioned it. For every village he had set ablaze, he had prayed that this purge was cleansing the faith of corruption. Cleanse us, oh Lawgiver, that we might serve you in purity. He had believed in that holiness with all his heart.

name: Name
body: But as the years went by, the temple doors closed to the outcast, the so-called clergy hoarded knowledge and wealth, and the once-glorious capital became a stage for fanatics vying for supremacy. At first, Malekus could not—would not—see the spreading rot. He told himself that the Lawgiver demanded obedience. If the scrutators had hammered out decrees, he must follow them. If the Hierarch or Synod condemned a group as heretical, Malekus would lead an entire battalion to confront and crush it. Yet with each pyre lit, a small voice whispered in the back of his mind. What if these are still children of the Creator? Should they not be guided back to the Law rather than be burned? Malekus had buried that voice beneath vows of devotion. He could not risk doubt; doubt was a crack in the foundation of a righteous life. So, he pressed on, his faith unwavering on the surface, though each drop of blood spilled left a stain he could not entirely wash from his conscience. Over time, the faithful throng he once knew became a gaunt, suspicious congregation. Subtly, the warmth of communal worship gave way to harshness and mistrust. A growing paranoia led people to suspect that any neighbor might be secretly corrupt. The temple’s doors, once open to those in need, were slammed shut to all but a chosen few. And now, those chosen few had splintered, turning against one another, until the entire nation was in a slow, deadly spiral.

name: Name
body:
Malekus’s breathing hitched as he recalled that first sermon, when everything had seemed so hopeful. He was little more than a terrified refugee from Caspia’s slums, bruised inside and out by a childhood filled with scorn. The evening sun poured through the windows, casting a jewel-toned light. The robed and masked priest had stood behind the altar, flanked by flickering braziers, his voice rising and falling like music.
"Children of Menoth," the priest had intoned, "He is the Lawgiver and the Creator of Man. Each drop of your sweat, each pang of your suffering, serves as a testament. Bear this with joy, for He sees you. The fires you endure in this life will burn away the impurities in your soul. Thus, if you suffer in His name, you are cleansed. If you sacrifice in His name, you are blessed."
The congregation had been filled with laborers in sweat-stained tunics, grieving widows clutching simple wooden Menofixes, and children who whimpered from hunger. Yet in that moment, as the priest’s voice echoed throughout the temple, every face had shone with a fervent glow. Malekus recalled how tears burned his eyes and how his arms had been covered in gooseflesh from the overwhelming sense of belonging. The priest—old even then, with a stooped stance—had lifted an arthritic hand in blessing.

name: Name
body: "Rejoice! Rejoice, for your suffering is forging you into true servants of His holy purpose. As we gather here, each of us is more precious to Him than the grandest palace. As we suffer, we are not alone, for He sees the truth within our spirits, and our shared pain will unite us, strengthen us, and lead us into the order He desires." The words had ignited a flame in Malekus’s chest. I am not worthless. That revelation had been momentous to him. His pain held meaning. Everything he had endured made him worthy in the eyes of his creator. He kept that memory close throughout his life, even now. But how foreign it had become after all these years. With a grunt, Malekus rose from his knees, his gaze still fixed on the tarnished Menofix. An indescribable ache throbbed within him, a longing for that old sense of clarity. He walked deeper into the temple, weaving around fallen candelabras and shattered pews. In places, the sand had piled so high that the floor was invisible. Rusted braziers lay scattered near a side chapel, the coal and incense long gone. Years of abandonment had transformed much of the interior into a mosaic of disrepair: cracks spread through the walls, and sunlight glinted harshly off shards of colored glass on the floor. High above, a stone depiction of Menoth’s stern figure in bas-relief had lost half its features to rubble. Now the Lawgiver appeared cleft in two, one half worn away by sand and time.

name: Name
body:
This temple had once been the heart of the faithful in the region. Pilgrims came for days of prayer and nights of reflection. The courtyard beyond had thrummed with conversation, priests and worshippers exchanging stories of hope and triumph. He could almost smell the fresh loaves distributed as alms to the poor who lined the temple steps—could hear the gentle hum of sacred songs.
No more. The courtyard outside was a husk of itself, scourged by the desert’s relentless fury. The battered statue of a hierarch lay toppled on its side, an arm broken off, and the figure worn featureless by scouring sand. War had come in waves: first, the crusades outward, then the internal strife. The city’s guardians had marched off to one conflict or another, leaving behind only disillusionment and lawlessness. Thieves stripped the temple of its valuables, carting away gilded icons or prying precious stones from its altars to sell on the black market. Meanwhile, the clergy who remained had grown paranoid, fearful, fracturing into factions that fought over the scraps of authority.

name: Name
body: We should have stood together, Malekus thought bitterly. We were once strong. Even the devout in Caspia feared the fervor of our faith. He remembered how proud he had been of the discipline, the order, and the sense of purpose. Now it was all undone, and he had no one to ask: Was it me? Did I fail you? Or did you, in your infinite power, decree that this was how it must be? Malekus walked back, his arms folded behind him. Behind the altar stood a grand dais where the priests had once declared laws and blessings to the devoted masses. The dais was carved with scriptural passages, each line detailing the commandments of the True Law: Honor the Creator, let your labor be an offering, let your pain be a sacrifice. However, the chiseling was chipped and weathered, making some words unreadable. It served as a metaphor for the entire theocracy, the entire land: once precise, now defaced and uncertain. Malekus mounted the steps of the dais, his boots grinding shards of colored glass underfoot. He realized how strange it felt to stand in this hallowed place without his ceremonial armor, lacking the mask and heavy breastplate that marked him as a leader among the Flameguard. And yet that was precisely why he had come in simple robes. He wanted no barrier between himself and the god he loved so dearly.

name: Name
body: He placed both hands on the chipped altar. The stone felt colder than he remembered. Once, it exuded warmth from the fires that burned constantly in the braziers beside it. Now it was lifeless, like a grave marker. He bowed his head until his brow touched the surface of the altar. "Please," he whispered, his throat tight, "hear my words. I am your servant, your weapon, your child. I have fought for you in countless battles. I have lit the cleansing flame that consumed your enemies. I have offered my flesh and blood to the fire as a testament to my faith. I did all these things because I believed they pleased you and upheld your Law. Yet now, we stand in ruins. Your people have been torn apart. Your temples are deserted. Your scriptures lie in tatters. Was I mistaken in my zeal? Have I angered you?" He drew a shaky breath. "Lord of humanity, you molded us from the waters and sand when the land was new. I’ve always believed that dust has purpose—we have purpose. But I see so much wasted life now, so many fatherless children, so many grieving widows, so many orphans. I used to think the orphans would gather here to learn discipline and piety in your name. Now, they roam the streets in packs, surviving on scraps. And the priests who remain…" He closed his eyes, remembering the cruelty he’d witnessed from those he’d once idolized and the nobility of those he'd once believed lacked sufficient zeal. How eager the priests were to sink their fangs into Menites who craved security, and how ready the Order of the Wall was to sacrifice their lives to protect that rabble. "The priests who remain stoke the flames of hatred instead of unity. They twist your word to justify their power."

name: Name
body: Memories tormented him: standing in bloodstained streets, reciting psalms as he set fire to a building that housed so-called heretics—the screams. The old sense of righteousness he’d felt then—he could not recapture it. Instead, he felt nauseated. Were they heretics? Or were they merely souls seeking a different path, perhaps a gentler path under your law? "I was told they were heretics," he continued softly, as if explaining to an unseen judge. "I was told your will demanded their sacrifice. Was it truly your will? Or was it the will of men who claimed to hear your voice?" His breath caught in his throat. "I prayed before every conflagration, prayed that the flames would purify and renew. That from the ashes, a stronger, more faithful people might rise. But all that rose was the stink of burning corpses." He raised his gaze to the tarnished Menofix mounted on the wall. Even with the metal’s luster gone, the shape remained painfully familiar—a reminder that once, this symbol gleamed above every city temple, proclaiming the One True Faith.

name: Name
body: "Speak to me," Malekus pleaded. "Give me a sign, however small. Send me a whisper on the wind. Let me feel the heat of your sacred flame again." The wind stirred in the shattered windows, and a faint swirl of sand danced across the dais. Malekus held his breath. But only dust settled across the cracked altar. A shudder of despair coursed through him. "Do I not deserve an answer?" he asked, voice raw. "After all I have done in your name… did I not do it for you?" He almost choked on the question. His tears dripped onto the sand-dusted stone. He was given no reply. He remained in this gutted temple, on his knees again, begging for the same thing. Show me. Show me you have not forsaken us. His clenched fist pounded the altar. A small, sharp crack rang out as he struck the stone, and flakes of ancient plaster chipped away. "How many times?" he demanded, voice ragged. "How many times did I ask your guidance before marching into another campaign of bloodshed?" He pressed his forehead to the altar’s cold surface. "I can bear the suffering if it’s your will, but I can’t bear not knowing."

name: Name
body: He let out a choked sob. Hot tears burned a path down his cheeks, stinging with the acrid grit of sand. A shameful voice in his head whispered that maybe the Creator had indeed abandoned them. Why not? Over the centuries, people’s devotion waxed and waned. Perhaps the Creator, in His infinite wisdom, had simply decided he didn’t believe in them either? "I beg you," he whispered hoarsely, "if silence is my punishment, I don’t know if I can bear it." He gripped the edge of the altar, knuckles whitening. "I’ve stood in your name on many battlefields. I’ve carried your banner into the heart of foreign lands. Why am I alone here?" His last words echoed miserably under the high arches before dying into the wind. He lifted his head in sudden fury. "Answer me!" The force of his shout startled him. The Menofix on the wall behind the altar stared down at him, silent and unmoved. Malekus choked on his final question, his emotions flooding up to strangle his words. He ground his teeth and choked back his tears before he felt strong enough to ask: "Why did you abandon us? What did we do?"
